I think the use of “pretentious” is incredibly annoying and turns me off most comments (matched by “overrated”) when talking about film. I personally never understood why people felt the creation section of Tree of Life was in-proper to have in there. To me it is not only some of the most gorgeous images put to film but more importantly it aligns with the creation and evolution of nature and perhaps the birth or one of the first acts of grace. The way of Nature and the way of Grace are the main themes of the film. 🤷🏻

Terrence Malick is probably my favourite filmmakers. People seem to get upset at his films but they are unique and beautiful. It is fantastic he is able to make his films how he wants. There are plenty of formulaic films out there, Malick continues to play with form and narrative and I love him for it. The music he uses is exquisite and I look forward to his film music almost as much as the film. It was tremendous fun to find all the amazing music in Tree of Life. 

So no, I reject he is pretentious. 😉

I am also an admirer of Malick’s films. The Tree of Life, to me, is one of the greatest films I have ever seen. Deeply moving, spiritually powerful, and possibly the finest articulation of Malick’s cinematic language, style.

However, looking at his filmography as a whole, I do believe Terrence Malick suffers from self-indulgence and image polishing. Especially after Tree of Life, his style suffers from self-parody and gimmick, like actors stirring around each other and whispers and beautiful naturalistic images. 

I think Tarkovsky on the other hand, perfectly embodies this transcendental style that Malick aspires to in his work. Everything in a Tarkovsky film is made significant, dare I say spiritual - nature, destruction, war, eroticism, innocence. Malick has a much limited tonal bandwith for exploring these matters of life, compared to Tarkovsky.

Also, can someone please recommend me contemporary filmmakers like Malick who approach films from a Christian pov? Would really love to see their work, especially if it is anti-transcendental lol.

“Nothing is so terrible as a pretentious movie. I mean a movie that aspires for something really terrific and doesn’t pull it off is shit, it’s scum…and everyone will walk on it as such. And that’s why poor filmmakers in a way – that’s their greatest horror – is to be pretentious. So here you are on one hand that’s trying to aspire to really do something, and on the other hand you’re not allowed to be pretentious. And finally you say, ‘fuck it.’ I don’t care if I’m pretentious or not pretentious or if I’ve done it or I haven’t done it. All I know is that I am going to see this movie. And that for me it has to have some answers. And by answers I don’t mean just a punch line, answers on about 47 different levels.“ - Francis Ford Coppola
All 47 levels of Megalopolis finally make sense to me after reading this quote.

I admit I’ve never engaged with Malick’s work as I just got the vibe that I wouldn’t enjoy them. That was until last month I saw Days of Heaven. I was truly blown away and it was a film I couldn’t stop thinking about. So many scenes and images that stick with me. 

I watched it on the Criterion Channel and there was some special features including interviews with the cast. I watched one with Sam Shepherd and he described Malicks films as poetry. There’s a feeling that comes through that you can’t quite describe but you understand through the themes and imagery. I thought that was a great insight. Can’t wait to watch more of his work soon.

I love telling this story:

I was teaching after school at a middle school in rural Texas, 90% hispanic, most kids have immigrant parents or are immigrants themselves. I ran the filmmaking club. We had a blast, those kids ruled.

Anyhoo, one day our star actor, Trinity, was absent. We were counting on her to shoot some of our project that day so we had to push and do something else. Annoying, but we had the time to spare and I often have backup plans in case of something.

The next day Trinity comes up to me and says "I'm sorry I was gone, but it was because I was at my grandma's and they were shooting a movie there!" and I said "that's cool!" like maybe a commercial or an indie or something and she said "look I got autographs" and she pulls out an actor I don't recognize, Natalie Portman, and the last one says "To Trinity - follow your dreams - Terence Malick" and I just pretty much freaked the f out.

I said "this is one of the most important directors working today - did you get his picture" and she said "no he wouldn't let me." And I nodded, understanding completely. She also said "it was exactly like how we do it, only way slower."

Anyway, I love that story. Little 6th grade Mexican chica Trinity got some face time with Terrence Malick. I later learned the scene was for "Song to Song" and had eventually been cut from the film.

I just had the pleasure of watching A Hidden Life & I found it to be incredibly moving and an important watch given the same type of turmoil in today’s world. It saddens me that it is not well known … the music, cinematography and scenes in nature are nearly transcendent.

I’ve only seen pieces of Malick’s other work and I’m inspired now to watch more. Any recommendations?
Tree Of Life, To The Wonder and The New World. All beautiful and hypnotic

He’s definitely my favorite filmmaker that still makes movies, hopefully he still has some films in him.
I remember when I first watched the Tree of Life, I got goosebumps, and that rarely happens. To describe his movies, I would say they are a visual representation of a journal or someone’s thoughts.
Best new movie I’ve watched in the last 10 years.

He's a legend, Badlands, Days of Heaven, Thin Red Line, Tree of Life. Everything after that gets a bit wonky for me but I would've been one of the kids who was like "What is this Ben Affleck movie about never heard of it." and  then watched To the Wonder and been baptized into the church of Malick.
Thank you for posting this brilliant story. I laughed about twelve times and smiled thru all of it. Just perfect.

The New World is one of my favorite films ever made. My friend met him at our local film festival years ago and said he’s most likely on the spectrum. His wife was his person, for the meet and greets and social stuff.

Singular artist that, you the viewer, have to put some effort into in order get onto the wavelength of the vision he’s trying to transmit. I feel that his first five films are all bonafide masterpieces, and that afterwards, his vision got somewhat lost in the static—though he seemed to have regained some of his mojo with A Hidden Life. I love how there’s usually an “explanation” on why the imagery is so unnaturally beautiful in his films, like with Days of Heaven, in the oft-suggested notion that it feels like we’re experiencing the story through the golden lens of nostalgia with Linda seemingly narrating the story many years after they occurred. Or with The Thin Red Line, with the notion that Scorsese espoused in that we’re witnessing everything through the lens of a unified soul, which also explains the mismatched voiceovers of the characters speaking over another’s perspective.

Let’s not overlook the way he completely changed the use of voiceover either, as I’m sure the prevailing notion of its artistic use before him was akin to Brian Cox’s portrayal of Syd Field in Adaptation proclaiming: “God help you if you voiceover in your work! God help you! It’s flaccid, sloppy writing.” Malick seemed to twist the use of voiceover from something mainly used to directly point out or emphasize something, or give added context to something (including the loathsome use of directly illuminating a character’s inner thoughts), into something that ever-so-gently buffets and supports the (magnificent) imagery with detached, philosophical musings that end up forming a kind of parallel, shadow narrative completely separate from the wispy-thin remnants of a plot that simply plods on forward as expected. It’s a delicate co-weaving of multiple narrative strands, and when it works (like in his first five films) the results can be transcendent.

It's weird to me that Malick is considered pretentious by so many people. It's like calling a landscape artist pretentious. His movies are largely just a celebration of the beauty of the natural world. Yes, you can read into how the images are presented and there is depth to his films,, but on a basic aesthetic level, they are just great to watch.

wouldnt't be a malick story if it didnt involve someone getting cut from the movie.  I wonder how the editing went for his new movie which filmed 5 years ago, pre covid....

Mr. Malick has given us two magnificent films:  **Badlands** (1973) & **Days of Heaven** (1978).  It says something about that great era that Hollywood studios would even risk such projects.

When he returned to filmmaking in 1998, he gave us the glorious mess of **A Thin Red Line**.  I suspect that there was indeed a great film somewhere in those hundreds of hours of footage he shot, but he never found it.  His later **Tree of Life** (2011) has a fine little coming-of-age-in-rural-Texas movie buried under a barrage of nature shots (it also has a puzzling final twenty minutes).  Both **Knight of Cups** (2015) & **A Hidden Life** (2019) are interesting little films, but the rest of his movies can, in my opinion, be skipped.

Mr. Malick has a great eye for natural beauty and shot composition.  He can coax some fine performances from real actors (but he has little success with non-actors such as Affleck and Farrell).  He has some difficulty with structure, which is odd since he made a good living for decades as a Hollywood 'script doctor'.  In short, he has his strengths and his weaknesses, but I've never considered his works to be 'pretentious', just spiritually ambitious (you know, like so many other American films of the last 50 years).

Malick is hit and miss for me. I love Badlands and The Thin red Line. For Days of Heaven I love the cinematography as most people do. the movies from the latter half aren't really for me. But I will say, even if I happen to not be into a particular story every movie he makes has something good to look at.

*The Tree of Life* is not only my favourite Malick film but possibly my favourite ever film by anyone. I adore that film so much. And it's so endlessly rewatchable. It somehow manages to capture a small-town fifties sensibility, the rigid gender dynamics of many suburban American families back then, along with the struggle to transcend them, as well as the most lavish cosmic context you'll ever see in any film that succeeds in portraying both. It's a poetic masterpiece and a loving exposé of humanity's beguiling side and hidebound side.

That said, aside from *A Hidden Life* and *Song to Song*, both of which have many strengths and which I enjoyed greatly, *The Tree of Life* might have been his pinnacle. I truly hope I'm wrong in that, although there's no shame in a filmography this beautiful, so please don't read this as criticism. He simply set a standard early in his career that by definition might be difficult if not impossible to surpass.

I really like Terrence Malick's work; his films often explore theological themes that resonate with me. The Tree of Life is essentially a loose adaptation of the Book of Job, and I love Witt’s character in The Thin Red Line, who is very much a Christian (at least that's how I see him) similar to Desmond Doss. His death scene is a masterpiece from both a directing and editing standpoint.

I've only seen his first four pictures and I can say I'm a huge admirer, I believe him to be an incredible unique filmmaker whose works typically try to unearth any shroud of humanity in an otherwise confused and hostile world. 

He's more focused in conveying the beauty of the human condition rather than sticking to a straight forward narrative and although I can see how that might put people off but theres just something about this approach that I find so moving and real about the characters in his pictures. 

In a way he's like the complete opposite of Nolan in that regards whose characters seem to lack any ounce of emotional intelligence.

Pretentious or not, his films make me sick. As in, literally nauseous. His constant camera movement mimics seasickness and destroys the experience for me. I can watch him on the small screen, but his movies are ones that should reward theatre-going, and I certainly think the man is talented with his cinematography. He just...doesn't hold the damn camera still. I really wanted to enjoy *Tree of Life*, too. It's frankly gimmicky that he employs this in every scene.

TLDR: nice shot, Terrence, now will you hold the camera still so I can enjoy it?
I recommend watching his earlier work. It’s fascinating to see him working things out and finding his style over time. Badlands, Days Of Heaven, and This Red Line are all fantastic.
The cinematography and nature in A Hidden Life are gorgeous. Too bad the Dolomites of Trentino don't look anything like the hills of Upper Austria.

Glad to find someone who takes Christianity and its artistic expression seriously and doesn’t immediately jump to edgelord atheist mode.

I like Malick enormously but he doesn't strike me as an intellectual filmmaker. Not to say that his philosophy not profound or that his effect is not comprehensible, but that he's motivated more by intuition, happenstance, and sometimes just chance. For example, I think Linda Manz's voice over in "Days of Heaven" was recorded in one take, with no script - it was just 15 year old Manz talking into a tape recorder for an hour; lay that over picture and voilà, Days of Heaven. Emmanuel Lubezki has mentioned over a few films that Malick set up a scene and the actors will be acting,  but then Malick will turn him while filming to follow a butterfly flying by. It's what saves him from pompousness and prentention, this dedication towards the little random detail, the momentary now.

It's infuriating how people see anything non-conventional in a movie as pretentious. I think it speaks to a larger problem with how people consume movies that they believe every scene and every shot has to be moving the plot forward. Malick's movies feel both grounded and ethereal in the way he uses nature to establish an atmosphere
Megalopolis was the distillation of that quote. Somewhere in the nearly 40 years he spent working on the film, Coppola went 'fuck it' and didn't care if it came across as a pretentious mess.

I think for a very significant number of people, movies aren't really anything more than easy-going entertainment. Superheroes, car chases, action, the typical thrill ride of a movie. I know one or two people that literally watch nothing but horror, some other people that are only into sci-fi. These people are into particular themes, not film in general. They don't want to sit through 3 hours of pretty pictures and then have to go do some reading to understand what they just watched.

I think a lot of people are missing out on potential films they would really enjoy. I know for myself I have specifically avoided films that I thought looked interesting for vapid reasons like "oh it has subtitles", then watched it years later and realized just what I was missing out on. I think mood/state of mind is important as well. I remember watching Tree of Life when it first came out when I was younger, and I was just completely lost. Years later I went back and watched it again and it blew my fucking mind and think I watched it another two or three times in a week.

From personal experience of having *tried* showing either foreign or more "artistic" films to people which had subject matter I knew they would find interesting, they almost always ended up being bored or unable to relate to the film.

>The voice overs in his films do grate on occasion 

What? Can you speak up, I can't understand a word of what you're saying, and it's very annoying. It's almost as if you're trying to make a point about the uselessness of the spoken word, which makes me wonder why you bother using it at all.

I think he has the most unique cinematic style ever and he’s perfected it. He constantly overwhelms me with beauty and feelings that are exclusive to his work. He’s not someone who’s films I would ever want to analyze or write about at length, just experience over and over again.

I don't think he's pretentious, it's just how he feels the film should be made. His work isn't for everyone, but no one's work is for everyone. He has a distinct style and the cinematography and feeling is what makes me love a Malick project. Although the scripts/plots can leave alot to be desired at times, his films always look good and they are always unique.

I'm not sure why you got buried in downvotes here. I disagree with you, but I appreciate a strongly held contrary opinion and this comment reads like it's coming from someone with a deep love of film. 

I see where you're coming from, particular about the ending of Tree of Life. I see what Malick is doing here and I want to embrace it, but the preceding Sean Penn sections feel under-cooked in a way that keeps me at arm's length during the emotional finale. The idea is clear enough, but the film depends too heavily on a sympathetic viewer to fill in the blanks, instead of fleshing out the present-day scenes to a satisfying degree. 

Or maybe I just have anti-Penn bias. To be clear, I love that ToL is framed by a grand thesis about nature & grace and attempts to connect the main story to this idea; I think the film is still stronger for including the dinosaurs, office building, and afterlife scenes, even if they don't entirely work for me. I just wish Malick had given us a bit more to grab onto with the present-day scenes, and done more to connect that little boy in Texas to the adult he wants us to care about in the finale.

Thanks, although the first part of your comment is puzzling. I've been watching Malick movies since 1978 when I was fortunate enough at a relatively young age to see *Days of Heaven* on the big screen, and I've seen *Badlands* and all of his films numerous times, so why would you think that I think 2011's *Tree of Life* was his first? I went back and reread my comment, and I can't see why you misunderstood me.

I was basically saying that Malick's filmography through *The Tree of Life* is almost perfect; his output since has been good, sometimes very good, occasionally great, but a lot patchier.

I was just confused by this part of your comment: 

“He simply set a standard early in his career that by definition might be difficult if not impossible to surpass.” 

I thought that you were referring to The Tree of Life with that “early” part - I was thinking “hmmm? The Tree of Life is great, but it’s the fifth Malick movie”. 

But now I realize that I misread your comment - my bad. Sorry about the confusion!

No worries, and now I think I see the source of our confusion. I think of his "early career" as everything up until 2011, but of course, you could argue that his early career ended with *The Thin Red Line* or *The New World*. It's a convenient division into two groups of five. But also, for me—and I realize how subjective this can be—TToL marks the end of a slightly more graspable narrative style, however lyrical and poetic, that shifts after 2011 into something more abstract. I still get plenty out of his "later" career, but it's not quite the same for me (aside from the usual Malick signature elements, I love *Song to Song* for slightly different reasons and *A Hidden Life* for how relevant it feels).

I haven’t seen Song to Song, but A Hidden Life is GREAT! 

I generally think of “early Malick” as the period that included Badlands & Days of Heaven - and to be fair, I think that you can definitely see a shift in his style after Days of Heaven. Not trying to knock Malick at all - but Badlands & Days of Heaven operated on a smaller, more intimate scale in comparison to The Tree of Life (for example). Badlands & Days of Heaven are much more grounded too, along with having a stronger emphasis on narrative. Both of those films presented Malick’s style in a more subtle way too…..whereas The Tree of Life is bigger, bolder, more abstract & much more ambitious/“epic” even…..and that’s before you got into the cosmic undertones of that film! 

And you can see a “slice of life” thread in Badlands & Days of Heaven too…..those ones depicted the day to day lives of folks in a rather intimate setting, rather than the huuuuuge, (again) epic experiences that you’d get with The Tree of Life.

You're not wrong. And we had to wait a long time for his third feature. Although I'd argue that *The Tree of Life* successfully braided the style of his earliest films with the more impressionistic style of his later films. To coin a phrase, it really ties the room together. And more seriously, for me, it does so seamlessly and sublimely. I was as entranced by Jessica Chastain's spinning around gnarly trees with butterflies as I was by a raptor showing rudimentary empathy toward another raptor or a truck spraying DDT while neighbourhood kids played in the clouds. (And I don't want to portray Chastain solely as some kind of disembodied and unattainable force of pure femininity, because her depiction of grief in those scenes was as gut-wrenching and visceral as anything I've seen.) 

Malick also went all out with a soundtrack that happened to coincide with so much music I was listening to at the time (Tavener, Górecki, Preisner among so many glorious choices), and in any other film would have been seen as bombastic overkill, yet worked so well for the cosmic sequences. 

I also loved Pitt's surprisingly subtle performance of a man wrestling with the toxic masculinity of his time and suppressing his own keen sense of beauty, not to mention the complicated influence that had on his boys. I could go on forever about that film. 

I'll speak up for *Song to Song*. It's vaguely about a love triangle of people in the music industry, but what stood out for me was again the musical aspects, Malick's keen sensibility in that regard. As a quick example, he distills the pure melancholy from such a familiar song—Del Shannon's "Runaway," which has almost become a movie placeholder for a certain kind of Americana—in a way that few others would have considered. And the musician cameos are one thing, with Patti Smith having the weightiest of them, but I also think Gosling and Portman and Mara were wonderful, with Fassbender and Blanchett also compelling. (I mean, that *cast*!)

And Lubezki's cinematography is possibly at its most singular and astonishing. So many [indelibly beautiful images](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=osNA33gKBd8). 

So I think we're kind of agreeing that his earlier films were slightly more linear (it's Malick, so this is relative!), his later films more abstract, while I'm arguing that *The Tree of Life*, perhaps because it's chronologically smack in the middle of his filmography, was successful in that it combined those two impulses so well. (This is admittedly a little simplistic, but it's kind of the gist of what I was trying to say.)

I just watched “To the Wonder” yesterday. It’s true, Malick’s films do not cater to the lowest common denominator. However, I love his work. The cinematography, his focus on a certain slice of American life (in many cases juxtaposed with Europe), the lighting (seems like it is always golden hour in his films), his use of a single camera, the minimal dialogue, and his preoccupation with the divine, etc. I always find his work thought-provoking and aesthetically gorgeous. I intend to watch “Days of Heaven” next.
